Universal prevention

Universal prevention interventions are for all children and young people.

Information and education

Alcohol and drug services play an important role in supporting their local communities. They provide accurate, relevant and timely information about the health harms of alcohol and drugs to every child and young person. This should include helping local education providers with their:

alcohol and drugs policies

lesson plans

The PSHE Association has developed lesson plans on drugs education.

Reducing risk and strengthening protective factors

The United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime and the World Health Organization’s International standards on drug use prevention suggest that universal prevention approaches for children and young people focus on reducing risk and strengthening protective factors. These approaches are more effective than topic-specific programmes and interventions. A wider prevention strategy should include a focus on:

school attendance

positive relationships

meaningful activities

Approaches that are least effective include:

knowledge-only approaches

scare tactics and images

using people with lived experience of dependence or the police as drug educators where their input is not part of a wider prevention programme

Targeted prevention

Targeted prevention is targeted towards children and young people at increased risk of alcohol or drug-related harm. It aims to reduce their risk of harm and strengthen their protective factors.

Harm reduction

Targeted prevention interventions should include age and context appropriate harm reduction for all children and young people, including advice and information on:

the spread of blood-borne viruses

sexual and reproductive health, including local chlamydia screening, condom provision, early pregnancy testing and unbiased pregnancy options advice

overdose risk and prevention, including naloxone supply where appropriate, in line with the guidance Supplying take home naloxone without a prescription

health harms and reducing risky behaviour

Care pathways should be in place for children and young people to access age-appropriate sexual health services and testing and treatment for blood-borne viruses.

Needle and syringe programmes, such as those provided in pharmacies, should operate in line with National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) public health guideline Needle and syringe programmes. They should also work to policies that have been agreed with the Families First Partnership programme and local safeguarding children’s partnerships.

Delivering targeted prevention interventions

Targeted interventions can also be delivered to children and young people with alcohol or drug problems who may not feel ready to engage with services. Where children and young people meet the threshold for a specialist intervention, specialist alcohol and drug services and partner agencies may offer:

screening or triage sessions

joint assessments

Targeted prevention interventions should be delivered by skilled staff who children and young people believe are knowledgeable and credible. They should be available in a variety of settings, including:

schools

youth hubs

primary care settings

For 16 to 24 year olds, services should consider appropriate place-based settings, such as:

further and higher education providers

festivals

night-time economy venues, such as pubs and bars

local community hotspots, such as youth clubs, community centres and Best Start Family Hubs

Working with children and young people at risk

Targeted prevention interventions should be delivered in partnership with services working with ‘at-risk’ groups. These groups include children and young people:

in care and care leavers

who have been exploited, abused or neglected

who are not in mainstream education or are NEET

who are experiencing mental health problems

with special educational needs and disabilities

Supporting children affected by parental alcohol or drug use

Some children and young people’s alcohol and drug services, and some children and family services, provide targeted interventions for children and young people whose parents or carers have alcohol or drug problems. These services provide this type of child-centred family support work whether or not the children themselves are using substances or the parent or carer is receiving treatment for their alcohol or drug problem. Child-centred family support work helps:

safeguard children

promote their health and emotional wellbeing

prevent future substance problems

Children should be guided by a professional to explore and understand their feelings and experiences of parental alcohol or drug use. Family members should also be supported individually and collectively to reduce the risk of harm and strengthen their protective factors.

Comprehensive capabilities for the drug and alcohol family support workforce are outlined in NHS England’s Capability framework for the drug and alcohol treatment and recovery workforce.

Specialist drug and alcohol interventions

Specialist drug and alcohol interventions refer to packages of care-planned support delivered in the community. They are tailored to children and young people who are experiencing harm related to their alcohol or drug use. Interventions are primarily psychosocial but can also be pharmacological and should include harm reduction advice.

Specialist interventions should be in line with:

‘Drug misuse and dependence: UK guidelines on clinical management’ - section 7.10 ‘Young people’

‘Clinical guidelines for alcohol treatment’ - chapter 23 ‘Specialist alcohol interventions and support for children and young people’

Alcohol and drug services should ensure that children and young people understand how they can self-refer into alcohol and drug services. This includes a communications plan that uses social media and targets children and young people, as well as important stakeholders and referrers.

What young people think a good service looks like: case study

The ‘Lived experience voices’ initiative run by Revolving Doors gathered the views of young people with lived experience and young ambassadors, with the help of service providers. Young people were asked what a good service for children and young people would look like.

They told us that services should:

have dedicated hubs that combine treatment, prevention and creative activities, providing a safe, accessible space within communities

use inviting, homely spaces - with both informal and private spaces - in multipurpose buildings

offer activities that are fun, therapeutic and available in both indoor and outdoor spaces

consistently involve young people in developing and implementing strategies and policies

offer peer support, especially from those with lived experience

have a strong social media presence managed by young people

provide an app for young people, parents and professionals

do outreach at events like raves and festivals

provide education and support for parents, including drop-in sessions and resources to help them understand and support their children

make transitions to adult services smooth, removing barriers to access them and ensure they are young person-centred

start universal education early, using age-appropriate content that focuses on harm reduction and realistic portrayals of the consequences of drug use

improve joint working and develop good relationships with other agencies

be empathetic, non-judgmental and focused on understanding the reasons behind young people’s actions

5. A skilled workforce

Children and young people’s feelings about the quality of their relationships with adults and peer mentors contribute significantly to their wellbeing and positive outcomes.

So, the therapeutic relationship children and young people have with their keyworkers is vital.

Capability framework and training curriculum

Delivering high-quality and effective interventions depend on a skilled workforce. In 2025, NHS England published the ‘Capability framework for the drug and alcohol treatment and recovery workforce’. This capability framework supports commissioners and service providers to develop a multidisciplinary workforce that can consistently deliver high-quality services. It identifies core capabilities for children and young people’s alcohol and drug workers, as well as 10 other core roles, including family support workers.

Children and young people’s drug and alcohol service commissioners, employers and service managers should use the capability framework and the new curriculum to ensure their workforce has the required skills, knowledge and behaviours.

They should also meet the following principles.

Training and development

Training and development for commissioners should be in place to ensure they are competent to commission safe and effective services for children and young people.

Service specifications should clearly indicate the level of professional competence required to deliver safe and effective services for children and young people.

Service providers should consider the specific training and continuous professional development needs of their workers, including:

the specific age and development needs of children and young people and the ways they differ from those of adults

age-appropriate evidence-based psychosocial and pharmacological interventions for children and young people

Supervision and workforce plans

Service providers must ensure that their workers receive mandatory safeguarding supervision. There should be a good model of supervision that supports caseload management but also reflective practice to identify worker development needs and wellbeing.

Treatment providers should have workforce plans that describe how specialist staff are trained and supported to make sure they are competent and supervised to deliver specialist interventions for children and young people.

Professionals in the workforce

A range of medical and health and social care professionals should be a part of the workforce, who provide clinical and system leadership and support. This includes:

doctors

nurses

consultant and practitioner psychologists

social workers

Services should also have good links to, and partnerships with:

sexual health workers

youth offending workers

mental health workers

Reciprocal training

Reciprocal training between alcohol and drug teams and other local practitioners working with vulnerable children and young people should be delivered. This will help to ensure that:

children and young people’s alcohol and drug workers have a comprehensive and up-to-date understanding of multiple support needs, referral pathways and legislative responsibilities

partner agencies understand alcohol and drug related stigma, behaviour and related problems, and screening and referral skills

Reciprocal training should include the following services:

children’s social care

mental health

youth offending

education providers

Online learning in North Yorkshire: case study

North Yorkshire Horizons drug and alcohol service has developed an online learning platform called the Drink Drug Hub. Launched in March 2022, any professional from across the county can access resources, including free drug and alcohol awareness training. The training is evidence-based and developed in collaboration with partner agencies and experts.

be a child social worker or a worker from another partner agency, should make sure that a transition plan is co-ordinated across all relevant services. The plan should involve the young person, as well as their parents or carers where appropriate.

Different services, such as youth offending teams, CAMHS and statutory children’s services, transition young people at different ages or developmental stages. These different arrangements should be detailed in the transitional care plan, so that everyone knows which agencies are involved, what support they are providing and when it is due to end.

Young people with care experience and those with EHC plans have legal entitlements to receive support for education, health, housing and life skills up to age 25. This can include remaining in a children and young people’s alcohol and drug service.

Children and young people’s alcohol and drug services are responsible for making sure that young people in their care are prepared for the transition to an adult alcohol and drug service. Where it is safe and appropriate, parents or carers should also be prepared for the transition.

Both children and young people’s and adult alcohol and drug services are responsible for making sure young adults receive continuous support. As a minimum, each service and the young person should review and update the final care plan before transition. Where possible, parents or carers should be involved in transition planning.

Supporting young people not in education, employment or training

Children and young people who are NEET, or who are at risk of becoming NEET, should receive co-ordinated support.

As part of their assessment and care planning, services should understand a young person’s education, employment and training status and any barriers to participating in them.

Where appropriate, services should establish pathways to education, employment and skills support, including individual placement and support (IPS) services. IPS is an evidence-based approach that helps people find and stay in work alongside treatment and recovery support.

A recent report on the outcomes of IPS found that 62% of people aged 24 and under who accessed IPS moved into employment, and around three-quarters of those who found work stayed in it for more than 13 weeks.

As well as supporting people into work, IPS can help young people start or return to education, training and apprenticeships. Participating in education, training and employment can support recovery and a successful transition to adulthood.

Employment support in South Tyneside and Gateshead: case study

Emerging adults aged 16 to 24 with alcohol or drug problems can face unique challenges when entering employment. These include:

uncertainty about career goals

balancing education and work

managing personal barriers, such as trauma, neurodiversity and mental health problems

South Tyneside and Gateshead councils have a dedicated IPS employment specialist for young people aged 16 and over. This ensures individually tailored support that enables young people to thrive in the workplace.

The employment specialist sits within the young person’s treatment team and works closely with recovery workers. They also work with a range of other partners as required, including:

social care and safeguarding teams

the young person’s education provider

training and apprenticeship providers

the young person’s family

The standard IPS model is adapted to recognise that young people:

often need more time and flexibility

may simultaneously need support to stay in or return to education

may want to explore work opportunities that include educational elements

may benefit from family involvement, where appropriate

This approach allows the employment specialist to support young people into sustainable employment by addressing their specific challenges.

Increasing engagement with alcohol and drug treatment services in Derbyshire: case study

Derbyshire County Council has developed a dedicated service for emerging adults called 1625 Outreach, delivered by Change Grow Live. It is a multi-component, community-based model designed to increase access and engagement from 16 to 25 year olds who would not typically use alcohol and drug treatment services.

The service relies heavily on integrated partnership working to operate from a range of age-appropriate, place-based settings, including:

night-time economy venues, such as pubs and bars

festivals and other large, organised events

further and higher education settings

community hotspots like youth centres

The service provides targeted, responsive support through a range of innovative engagement methods, including pop-up stalls, education workshops and a mobile unit. Digital outreach is also an important feature, using a range of social media platforms to promote age-appropriate harm reduction content.

These targeted, early interventions aim to reduce illicit substance use and related risk-taking behaviours among 16 to 24 year olds that are at increased risk of experiencing alcohol or drug-related harm. The service also acts as an accessible first point of contact for those who may need more structured treatment, with direct referral pathways into both young people’s and adult alcohol and drug services in Derbyshire.

In 2025, the service engaged 6,312 young people aged 16 to 24 across these place-based settings. Of these:

44% had used cocaine

43% had used ketamine

36% had used nitrous oxide

A total of 76 referrals were made into treatment services for continued, care-planned interventions.

A feasibility study to evaluate the 1625 Outreach service has been published on the ‘Our research’ page of the Change Grow Live website. Aspects of the model have since been adopted in Sheffield, Derby, Nottingham and Liverpool.
